items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: One day I was contacted by Billy Taylor to do a recording date with Fats Waller... The musicians were Billy Taylor Sr. (bass), Harry Dial (drums), Gene Cedric (clarinet & tenor) and myself.

ctx.x: After a few months at the Savoy, Teddy Hill and orchestra were engaged to play at the Ubangi Club which had been Connie's Inn and Harlem Club before. In place of having girls in the line up, there were six female impersonators and the main attraction was a lesbian named Gladys Lentley. Gladys was quite plump and wore a man's full dress suit for her act and dressed like a man except for a skirt when she had on street clothes. Gladys played piano, sang and tap danced a little.

Allen Drew was a cigar-smoking manager of ceremonies and comedian. A girl pianist and singer by the name of Una Mae Carlisle was also engaged at the club and she was a protege of Fats Waller when he was playing for the WLLW. radio station in Cincinnati.

The six female impersonators were not bad as chorus girls and some looked almost like girls. But later the manager added six more sissies and some of them had muscles like a prizefighter and they really looked funny in those chorus girls costumes and the big muscles showing in their arms and legs.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I told him about the recording session with Fats... The next session I did with him

ctx.x: Teddy asked me what was wrong and I told him about the recording session with Fats and how much I had drunk. We called Teddy 'Fess' as so many other orchestra leaders were called. So after hearing my story, Fess told me to go out and get some air for a while and come back later. I went out for half an. hour and came back, but I was not feeling any better as far as being able to play was concerned. So Fess told me to take the night off. I had seen a trumpet player named Ovie Alston going into the bar of Big John's…

I went into Big John's, saw Ovie and told him my troubles and asked him to finish the night for me. In that manner, Teddy's band was not without a third trumpet. I made it home without staggering and went to sleep as soon as I got undressed and into bed. And I had learned a lesson that I never forget, and that was never try and drink as much as Thomas "Fats" Waller. The next session I did with him, I drank, but not every time the bottle was passed to me.

After our run at the Ubangui Club, the band played a week at the Howard Theatre in Washington and an engagement in the Roseland ballroom and then came back to the Savoy. During that time I had gotten behind in my allimony payments and shortly after I had made the second record session with Fats, I received a notice to appear in the Domestic Relations court again and was ordered by the judge to pay 10 dollars a week until
